pages.englishTranslation:
The Datan Algal Reef

This is the Datan Algal Reef in Taoyuan, Taiwan. It is one of the few remaining living shallow-water algal reefs in the world.

The reef has many small holes and spaces. These spaces provide homes for many kinds of sea life, including fish, shrimp, crabs, and shellfish. Nearly 100 kinds of living things can be found here. That is why the algal reef is often called the “nursery of marine life.”
reviewNotes: Chinese fills upper page and reef art fills the rest.
pages.bottomStripText:
The Datan Algal Reef

This is the Datan Algal Reef in Taoyuan, one of the few remaining living shallow-water algal reefs in the world. Its porous terrain provides homes for many kinds of fish, shrimp, crabs, and shellfish. It nurtures nearly 100 kinds of living things and enriches the marine ecosystem, which is why it is called the “nursery of marine life.” Besides fish, shrimp, crabs, hermit crabs, octopuses, shellfish, and starfish, the reef is also home to precious and rare species such as moray eels, hammerhead sharks, sea lilies, Chai-shan cup corals, and green sea turtles.

pages.englishTranslation: Unlike coral reefs, which are built by animals, algal reefs are mainly formed by algae. At Datan, crustose coralline algae form hard layers of calcium carbonate over time. Algal reefs grow very slowly: it takes about ten years for the reef to grow just one centimetre higher. The Datan Algal Reef is more than 7,600 years old and needs our protection.
reviewNotes: Chinese explanation is above full reef artwork; no safe aligned box.
pages.bottomStripText: What is an algal reef? Unlike coral reefs, which are built by animals, algal reefs are built by plants. The Datan Algal Reef is formed mainly by crustose coralline algae. Through calcification, these algae deposit calcium carbonate and gradually build the reef. Research shows that it takes about ten years for the reef to grow just one centimetre. Our Datan Algal Reef has a history of more than 7,600 years.

Our Home Is in Danger!

Bobo quickly blew his horn to call all the sea animals together. “Big news! Very big news! A third liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal is planned for this area. Our home may be destroyed!”

pages.bottomStripText:
Our Home Is in Danger!

Bobo immediately blew his horn and gathered the sea creatures of the Datan Algal Reef: “Big news—huge news! A third natural-gas receiving terminal is going to be built here. Our home is going to be destroyed!”

The residents were alarmed and frightened. They asked one another, “What should we do? We’ve lived here for so long—where can we go?”

pages.englishTranslation:
Everyone was shocked and worried. “What should we do?” they asked one another. “We have lived here for so long. Where can we go?”

As part of the energy transition, an area near the Datan Algal Reef had been chosen as a site for an LNG receiving terminal. However, developing this part of the sea could seriously damage the algal reef and threaten the animals living there. The sea animals had called this place home for thousands of years. Where could they go if they lost their home?

Developing the marine area of the algal-reef ecosystem would seriously damage and threaten its ecology. After living here for thousands of years, where could the algal-reef residents go?

The Fairy’s Magic

That night, Bobo was so worried about moving that he could not sleep. He and his friends looked up at the stars to clear their minds. Just then, a shooting star streaked across the distant sky. “Look quickly—it’s a shooting star!” Bobo cried excitedly.

pages.englishTranslation:
The shooting star turned into a shining fairy. “I have heard all your worries,” the fairy said. “I am the fairy who protects this algal reef. I am here to help you!”

Bobo asked, “How can you help us? We can only live in the reef, not on land. Is there another way besides moving to find a new reef?”

pages.bottomStripText:
Then something magical happened! The shooting star became a glowing fairy and appeared before them. “I heard all your worries. I’m the fairy who protects this algal reef, and I’m here to help you!”

After hearing her, Bobo asked curiously, “How can you help us? We can live in the algal reef but not on land. Apart from moving to find a new reef, is there anything else we can do?”

You must return to the sea before sunset on the third day, or you will disappear forever!” After saying this, the fairy vanished into the night sky.

Help Before Sunset!

Day after day passed, and before they knew it, sunset on the third day had arrived. Bobo saw the sun about to sink into the sea and used all his remaining strength to shout, “Help! Help! Somebody, please come!”

Just then, some people passing nearby heard him and looked toward Bobo. “Look! There’s a boy over there who needs help!” they called.

pages.englishTranslation:
Everyone Can Help!

At last, people began to understand what was happening. They discovered that the Datan Algal Reef, which was facing development, was home to countless sea animals. It was a rich and important marine ecosystem. People began to ask whether the energy transition must come at the cost of this precious treasure, and how they could protect marine life and the Datan Algal Reef ecosystem.

Everyone Can Help!

Only then did people realize that the Datan Algal Reef, which was about to be developed, was home to countless sea creatures and a rich marine ecosystem. People began to reflect: must the energy transition come at the cost of this precious treasure? What can we do to conserve marine life and protect the Datan Algal Reef ecosystem?

pages.englishTranslation:
Preface

A Dream Begins and Comes Full Circle

Yong’an Fishing Harbor in Xinwu is Taiwan’s only Hakka fishing harbor.

Xinwu’s stone tidal-weir group is the largest on Taiwan’s main island. At least six weirs are still in active use. These precious living records have shaped the rich fishing culture of Hakka coastal villages.

The energetic Xinwu Hometown Association invited me to serve as a consultant. During an interpreter-training course, the association members were delighted to discover clusters of stone tidal weirs while looking for local cultural features. I immediately added basic field-research methods to the course. They then formed a 38-member survey team and spent half a year measuring, collecting materials, interviewing people, and searching for this valuable tangible cultural heritage, believed to have been passed down for 300 years. On 29 June 2013, they published “Legend of the Xinwu Stone Tidal Weirs: A Field Survey of Taiwan’s Largest Stone-Weir Group.” I was deeply honoured to be part of it.

Yet I also felt regret. Our younger generation may find field-survey reports difficult to understand and may have few opportunities to learn about the wisdom preserved in the stone tidal weirs left by our ancestors. So I began to weave a dream in my heart and set to work writing and illustrating for children.

I thank Ms. Lu Shumei and Ms. Emma Tsai for completing the Hakka and English translations; Mr. Xie Qiantong and Mr. Jacky Baltes for reviewing the Hakka and English text; the Hakka Affairs Council and Xinwu Township Office for their support; and Chairman Guo Xianzhang and the Xinwu Hometown Association for generously serving as the publication’s chief planner. These many kind connections have brought my dream to completion.

About Stone Tidal Weirs

A stone tidal weir is a fishing method that uses the tides. A long barrier is built on the shore with stones. At high tide, seawater flows over it and fish swim into the weir. As the tide ebbs, the water gradually recedes, leaving the fish trapped inside and easy to catch.

Building a stone weir requires a sturdy wall that can withstand the waves, as well as careful decisions about its height, direction, and location. If it is too high, fish may be trapped outside; if it is too low, fish inside may escape with the ebbing tide. Building one therefore takes extensive experience and specialized skill.

In the past, without machinery, building a stone weir was a huge undertaking. Families living near the coast pooled money and labor—sometimes dozens or even hundreds of people working together. They shared the catch, creating a way of life that reflected the hard work, wisdom, and cooperation of earlier generations. A stone weir is therefore a living piece of history.

Even after a weir was built, it required year-round work. Fishers had to go out at all hours to match the tides, and regularly patrol and repair sections damaged by the sea. Typhoons and giant waves could destroy a wall, making repairs especially difficult. In modern times, some builders have used excavators. At Xinwu in Taoyuan, construction waste was used to rebuild a weir with an excavator, preserving its function while creating an unusual “modern stone weir.” The contrast between old and new methods is fascinating.

Besides Penghu, stone weirs once dotted Taiwan’s northwestern coast and are believed to date back 200 to 300 years. Changes in water conditions, marine pollution, and declining fish stocks made fishing less rewarding, and many weirs gradually fell into ruin. Today, few remain. Xinwu has ten, six of which are still in use. They are among Taiwan’s most valuable surviving stone weirs and living teaching resources.

Comparing Penghu’s weirs with those on Taiwan’s main island reveals how people adapted to local materials. Penghu has abundant basalt and coral limestone, suitable for building high walls—some weirs rise like a Great Wall in the sea. On the northwestern coast of Taiwan, large cobblestones are less stable for building high walls. But the local waters produce abundant oysters and barnacles, which grow densely on the weirs and strengthen them. Stone weirs show how people learned to adapt to and make good use of their environment.

Coastal Nature Walk: Beautiful Plants and Animals in This Book

Squirrel — A familiar mammal in coastal windbreak forests. Though people may think squirrels damage trees by eating plants, they mainly eat insects and help maintain ecological balance. They are also adorable.

Stag beetle — Stag beetles, rhinoceros beetles, and other beetles are commonly found in coastal forests. With fewer natural habitats, these forests can become a refuge for beetles.

Sea sandbur — On sandy beaches and in open areas of windbreak forests, the wind may send little round balls rolling by. They are actually the fruits of a coastal plant, not toys.

Little egret — Often seen feeding on mudflats, this elegant white bird is sometimes regarded as a symbol of Taiwan’s countryside.

Black-naped oriole — Several kinds of orioles visit Taiwan. Some pass through on migration, while others stay. They often perch high in the branches.

Rhodomyrtus tomentosa — A coastal shrub with beautiful pink flowers and purple fruit. The fruit is edible and can be made into jam or a fragrant drink.

Red Crab — A red crab found in the windbreak forest. Its shell has two spots and a large curved line that look like a smiling face. It is a crab that helps the environment.

Yellow Hibiscus — Also called sea hibiscus or “rice-cake tree.” Its yellow, bell-shaped flowers can be cooked into a salad. Its heart-shaped leaves are ideal for wrapping rice cakes, and the cakes acquire a distinctive fragrance when steamed.

Sacred Ibis — Native to Central Asia, the sacred ibis was revered in ancient Egypt. About twenty years ago, a typhoon struck a wildlife park in northern Taiwan, and more than ten ibises escaped. They have since multiplied into a sizable population.

Beach Naupaka — Tolerant of heat and drought, this plant is suitable for seaside gardens. Its small white flowers look like half an umbrella, as if the other half had been cut away. Its edible fruit is a childhood treat that local people remember fondly.

Chinese Hibiscus — Also known as the red hibiscus, it is vigorous and easy to propagate from cuttings, and is often planted as a hedge. Its large, vivid flowers can be made into juice or delicious salads.

Crow — A common country bird, bold and aggressive, but also a farmer’s friend because it eats pests. It once perched on the backs of water buffalo; today it often follows plows and tractors to catch insects.

Black-crowned Night Heron — Also called the “night heron” in local speech and “dark-light bird” in Mandarin. It sleeps through much of the day and comes out at night to feed. Fish are its favorite food, and it often hunts in shallow water.

Mudskipper — A fish adapted to the muddy intertidal zone, able to feed both in the water and on land. It is a good indicator of environmental health; when an estuary becomes polluted, mudskippers disappear.

pages.bottomStripText: The Heartbeat of Stone: The Chambered Nautilus

Hey! Do you know what I am?

I am the chambered nautilus.
I am not a fossil!
I am not a fossil!
I am not a fossil!

I have already been living on Earth for a very, very long time.

I appeared in the oceans about 400 to 500 million years ago—long before most dinosaurs, and even before the earliest dinosaurs appeared on Earth!

Let’s take a closer look. How am I different from them?

I am an ancient mollusk, and there’s no other one quite like me!

The earliest written record of my name appears in a poem by the Southern Song poet Yang Wanli: “I’ll go into the sea to find a nautilus shell and bring it back to make a cup!”

Later, the Tang poet Li Shangyin wrote:

“A parrot-shell cup: thirty-six thousand days in a hundred years;
three hundred cups must be drunk each day!”

What an extravagant image!

The name “nautilus” may sound unfamiliar. In ancient Greece, people called a sailboat a nautilus. The shell of a nautilus looks a little like a boat with a sail.

You may be wondering: what do sailboats and nautiluses have in common?

Let me explain…

I’m the only living cephalopod with an external shell. Most of us live in the deep waters of the Indian and western Pacific Oceans, where the water is about 19–20°C.

We grow slowly. If nothing unusual happens, we may live for as long as 20 years!

Among cephalopods, I’m one of the longest-lived.
Although I look like an octopus or a squid, I’m actually very different from them.

First, an octopus has eight arms, while a squid has ten.

I have about ninety tentacles.

They have suckers on them.

I have about sixty to ninety tentacles. They have no suckers, but they do have mucus.

The outer tentacles are used for grasping. There are nineteen pairs; around the mouth, males have twelve pairs and females have twenty-four to twenty-six pairs.
Also, my eyes are very simple compared with an octopus’s or squid’s. I have only one pair of simple eyes, with poor vision. I mainly use smell and touch to sense the world around me.

Finally, because octopuses and squids have no shell, they can move at great speed when escaping an enemy.

But I have a hard shell that can grow to 22 centimeters across, so I move very, very slowly.
I’m a favorite food of sharks and other large fish.

To protect myself, I can only live in deep water—about 50–300 meters below the surface—and rise slowly toward the shallows at dusk or dawn.

I mainly eat small crustaceans, tiny fish, and shellfish found on the seafloor, as well as bits of dead marine animals.

There are many predators in the ocean.

Why can I float up and down in the sea?

That’s because the inside of my shell is divided into chambers of different sizes, arranged from large to small. The largest chamber is on the outside, and it is where my body lives. The other smaller chambers contain gas.

When fluid flows into my chambers, my body becomes heavier, so I sink.

When fluid flows back out, the chambers fill with gas, making my body lighter, so I can float back up.

Diagram labels: Siphuncle; chambers (partitions).

You may be wondering: how can I float up and down in the water?

The outer part of my shell has chambers arranged from large to small. The largest chamber is at the outside, and I can live in it. The other small chambers are filled with gas.

When the gas in my chambers decreases, my body becomes heavier, and I sink.

When the gas increases, my body becomes lighter, and I rise.

When my body becomes heavier, I can sink.

When my body becomes lighter, I can rise.

When the oxygen level in the water is low, I can stay still for a while to conserve energy.

So when an enemy attacks, I can quickly retreat into my shell to protect myself.

My main predators are large fish. Since I live in deep water, they can’t easily find me!

A chambered nautilus lays eggs only once a year.

It takes about a year for the eggs to hatch, usually in a crevice among coral reefs or on a rock.

It takes around twelve months for me to mature—longer than it does for humans.

I believe many people have seen me at public aquariums.

We often swim around and around, as if dancing for everyone.

Some people even want to raise us as pets.

Did you know? There have been successful cases of breeding chambered nautiluses in captivity, but no effective method has yet been found to increase their population through breeding.

Please imagine this: if people keep catching and selling chambered nautiluses, what will happen if we keep being caught and sold?

No more!

We should protect the chambered nautilus and other precious marine animals, and safeguard their habitats!
Therefore, I hope you’ll help spread the word about protecting the chambered nautilus!

Now that you’ve read about me, it’s quiz time!

Can you tell whether this picture shows a chambered nautilus?

Oops! I forgot to tell you: the chambered nautilus has many different colors. Its color helps it camouflage itself from predators, so I deliberately changed colors.

In real life, my colors should be reddish brown and white.

Have you heard of the SDGs?

In 2015, the United Nations adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Goal 14 is “Life Below Water.” It aims to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas, and marine resources.

Marine conservation needs everyone’s support. Protecting marine life and ecosystems, and learning about marine ecology and laws, are goals you can help achieve!

The ocean is home to countless living things. Let’s work together to protect it, so marine resources can be used sustainably.

Please do your part as a responsible global citizen and protect our ocean and our planet.

Protecting the Sea Rose — The Giant Clam

Created by Lin Kui-Ting

To encourage students at all school levels to combine marine-science outreach with art and literature, this marine-science picture-book contest was held to inspire creativity. The works were judged primarily on the ideas they conveyed. Although the winning entries were reviewed by expert scholars to correct their scientific content, scientific information changes over time, and some details may differ slightly from current understanding. Readers and educators are encouraged to consult further sources to ensure that the science they share is accurate.

Third Marine Science Picture-Book Creation Contest — Award-Winning Work

At Hualien Harbor, on Taiwan’s east coast, the coastal plain is narrow. Along the shore are rich coral-reef communities and tropical fish, while the intertidal zone is home to many kinds of seaweeds, fish, shrimp, shellfish, and other marine life…

Marine Tips
1. Green sea-turtle shells are usually coffee-brown, reddish-brown, or olive, though colors vary by species and individual.
2. The number of a jellyfish’s tentacles varies by species.
The intertidal zone is home to many kinds of seaweeds, fish, shrimp, shellfish, and other marine life. Among them is a group of clams known as the “roses of the sea.”

At Hualien Harbor, on Taiwan’s east coast, the coastal plain is narrow. Along the shore are rich coral-reef communities and tropical fish, while the intertidal zone is home to many kinds of seaweeds, fish, shrimp, shellfish, and other marine life…

Since the east coast began to be developed, visitor numbers have risen year by year, leading to the removal of many giant clams from the local reefs. In the past, members of the local Amis community also harvested giant clams for food.

People make giant-clam shells into necklaces and other ornaments, or sell the clams to aquariums for display.

People also remove and eat the adductor muscle (the clam meat) and the mantle (the mantle tissue).
Marine debris not only destroys the habitats of marine life; it can also cause animals to mistake trash for food and eat it.
Environmental pollution is another reason giant clams are disappearing. Global warming raises seawater temperatures, putting marine life at risk.

One day, while diving, a local Amis man named Ajie suddenly discovered traces of giant clams. He remembered how his elders had often told him about the abundance, beauty, and importance of giant clams in the sea when he was young.
Today, giant clams are becoming fewer and fewer. Some are even poached or traded, and piles of trash have taken over their home.

Before we learn how local people began their conservation program, let’s first get to know these “roses of the sea”—giant clams.

Giant clams (chē qú bèi in Chinese) are commonly called giant clams and, in Taiwan, “five-claw clams.” They live in the warm coral-reef waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. There are twelve giant-clam species worldwide. In Taiwan they are found in Penghu and along the east coast; seven species occur here: bear-paw (horse’s-hoof) clam, fluted or scaly giant clam, crocus or boring clam, small giant clam, giant clam, smooth or southern giant clam, and Noah’s giant clam.

They are bivalves that live in shallow coral-reef areas. Their elongated oval shells look much like those of ordinary clams. The shell is grayish white or ocher; the largest can exceed one meter and weigh about 500 kilograms, while even the smallest species reaches about 14 centimeters. Their wavy shells and vividly patterned, colorful mantles resemble beautiful petals, which is why they are called the “roses of the sea.”

Shell: Two valves, with an adductor muscle between them that controls opening and closing.
Foot: Extends to attach the clam to rock or coral.

Marine Tip: Scientific information changes over time; readers can consult related sources to learn more.

Symbiotic algae: zooxanthellae.

Eyespots: Detect light along the edge of the mantle.

Mantle: The colorful, patterned tissue between the two shells is where zooxanthellae live and photosynthesize.

Can you spot these seven kinds of giant clams in the wild?

In the past twenty years, Noah’s giant clams and small giant clams have been the most common and numerous. Only empty shells of the giant clam have been found on the seabed off Dongsha Atoll, and the smooth giant clam has not been seen. So only five kinds of giant clams are now found alive in the wild. Their average density there is very low—about fifteen per square kilometer. Restoration through captive breeding began in 2004, with groups also taking part in the work.

In diverse ecosystems, giant clams and corals are both animals that host symbiotic algae in their bodies. The algae provide nutrients through photosynthesis, enabling clams and corals to continue growing. Their shells and skeletons also add many suitable places for organisms to attach. This mutually beneficial relationship plays a direct and important role in stabilizing coral-reef ecosystems and indirectly supports many human uses as well.

Marine Tip: Scientific information changes over time; readers are encouraged to consult further sources.

Why do giant clams come in so many colors?

Their vivid colors have the same cause as coral: symbiotic zooxanthellae live inside them. Besides corals, sea anemones, radiolarians, flatworms, jellyfish, and giant clams also form partnerships with symbiotic algae. The clam provides a safe home for the algae; in return, photosynthesis produces sugars and other nutrients that supply about 90% of what the clam needs to grow, live, and reproduce. The remaining roughly 10% comes from filter-feeding. Most of a giant clam’s nourishment comes from the photosynthetic algae living with it, making it a mollusk that may not survive without sunlight.

What are symbiotic algae?

Until 2004, it was difficult to classify these algae by appearance alone. Advances in molecular biology allowed scientists to identify many groups. Scientists once thought each host had a single, highly specialized algal partner. We now know that one giant clam can contain several groups at once: usually one is dominant while the others are less common. The mix also varies with clam species, habitat, region, and stage of growth.

Marine Tip: Scientific information changes over time; readers are encouraged to consult further sources.

How do giant clams raise the next generation?

Giant clams are hermaphrodites. During the breeding season they release sperm first and eggs afterward. About 10–12 hours after fertilization, the eggs develop and hatch into free-swimming larvae. After about 30–40 hours, the larvae develop shells and begin filter-feeding. After roughly 6–12 days, they become juvenile clams with a foot. As they grow, juveniles swim intermittently and gradually settle near the bottom, eventually becoming young clams.

Giant clams grow very slowly at first; their growth rate increases after about a year, then slows again as they approach maturity. They reach about 21 cm after roughly three to four years.

Working together to protect giant clams

You may have heard that warmer seawater causes coral bleaching. Excessively warm water disrupts the symbiosis between zooxanthellae and coral. When the algae leave or die, the coral loses its bright colors. The same can happen to giant clams: without zooxanthellae they become bleached, with only their white shells remaining. If the algae do not return soon, prolonged bleaching can ultimately kill the clam.

Other threats include human poaching. Giant-clam shells and pearls are prized for their beauty, putting clams at risk of overharvesting and theft.

When Ajie returned home, he began thinking about how to protect this beautiful sea before it grew even more degraded. He gathered friends and people from the community to discuss ways to protect the ocean together.

Giant Clam Conservation Plan
1. Form a patrol team.
2. Prohibit harvesting.
3. Hold beach- and ocean-cleanup activities.

The community held an information session so local people could understand the plan and take part in conservation activities. Through summer-camp activities, children got to know giant clams firsthand. Experts were also invited to explain the subject and foster a vision of a sustainable ocean.
Ajie also invited local residents to form a marine patrol team. Their first task was to clean up the giant clams’ home.
They organized beach-cleanup activities and put up signs. This brought local residents together to take part and helped visitors learn about the project.
Another important task for the marine patrol team is to use photographs and video to count the giant clams in this sea area, map their locations, and monitor them.

After more than five months and over forty monitoring surveys, the team found 103 giant clams and created a record of them. Four species were found in this area: Noah’s giant clam, the small giant clam, the crocus clam, and the fluted giant clam.

Noah’s Giant Clam
The mantle has a blue, green, or brown base color with droplet-shaped markings; the eyespots along the edge are sparse. The shell has five to seven radiating folds, with scales on the folds and large byssal openings.

Crocus Clam
The mantle has a blue, green, or brown base color with spots or patches, and the eyespots along the edge are dense. The mantle has one dark or light ring pattern. The shell’s radiating folds bear scales, and the byssal openings are elongated ovals.

Fluted Giant Clam
The mantle has a blue, green, or brown base color with patch-like markings, and the eyespots along the edge are sparse. The shell has four to five radiating folds with well-developed scales, and the byssal openings are conspicuous.

Small Giant Clam
The mantle has a blue, green, or brown base color with spots or patches, and the eyespots along the edge are dense. The shell has four to six radiating folds with scales, and the byssal openings are large.

Along the shore, signs were put up and patrols conducted regularly. If visitors or residents were found harvesting giant clams, the team patiently explained the rules and encouraged them to join the conservation effort. Challenges remained: some community members did not understand the need for protection, and poachers still slipped in.

When everyone was feeling discouraged, a fierce storm suddenly struck. Some giant clams were poached, and many other marine creatures were also threatened. This made the community feel more deeply the vulnerability of nature and the importance of caring for it. More people then joined the marine patrol team voluntarily, helping keep watch over the giant clams and marine life.
Through everyone’s continued efforts, giant clams were no longer being poached. Baby giant clams gradually began to appear, and their numbers slowly increased…
With everyone’s ongoing care and restoration work, the marine environment became cleaner, and marine life and coral reefs became healthier too.

Your small contribution can bring great rewards for giant clams and this marine area. Let’s join hands and become “citizen scientists” together!

Since the end of 2022, community members have worked together to protect the clams and keep watch over them. Though they faced many challenges, they did not lose heart. Each trial made them more determined, so that the giant clams in this East Coast harbor community can live safely and sustainably.
